The integration of edge computing with artificial intelligence has emerged as a transformative paradigm in precision agriculture. This convergence addresses a critical limitation in conventional IoT-based farming systems: the reliance on cloud connectivity for data processing and decision-making. In many agricultural regions, particularly in developing economies, intermittent network connectivity and high latency render cloud-dependent architectures impractical for time-sensitive operations such as irrigation scheduling and plant health monitoring.

This study presents an integrated edge AI framework that combines local inference capabilities with sensor networks to enable real-time agricultural decision-making. The system architecture employs a Raspberry Pi 4 as the edge compute node, interfaced with an Arduino Uno co-processor for analog sensor data acquisition. Environmental parameters including soil moisture content, ambient temperature, relative humidity, and atmospheric pressure are monitored using calibrated sensors at ten-minute intervals. A Raspberry Pi Camera Module V2 captures visual data for plant health assessment using a convolutional neural network deployed via TensorFlow Lite.

The experimental design follows a three-zone configuration to evaluate system performance. The control zone operates under conventional timer-based irrigation. The stress zone receives reduced irrigation at seventy percent of the control volume. The AI-managed zone uses predictive irrigation scheduling driven by a Random Forest model trained on soil moisture dynamics, evapotranspiration estimates, and historical weather data. Roma VF tomato plants serve as the test crop across all three zones, providing consistent biological baselines for comparison.

Random forest models were chosen over more complex deep learning alternatives for several pragmatic reasons. First, they require substantially less training data to generalise effectively. Second, their feature importance rankings are directly interpretable, which simplifies debugging when the model behaves unexpectedly. Third, they execute efficiently on the Raspberry Pi 4's ARM Cortex-A72 processor without requiring hardware acceleration. The final model uses one hundred estimators with a maximum depth of twelve, trained on approximately three thousand labelled samples collected over a six-week period.

Preliminary results indicate that the AI-managed zone achieved a twenty-three percent reduction in water consumption compared to the timer-based control, while maintaining statistically equivalent plant health metrics. Soil moisture variance in the AI-managed zone remained within optimal ranges for ninety-four percent of the trial duration, compared to seventy-one percent for the control zone. These findings suggest that edge-based AI irrigation can meaningfully conserve water without compromising crop outcomes, even in resource-constrained deployment scenarios.

Several limitations warrant acknowledgment. The six-week trial period does not capture seasonal variations in weather patterns or crop growth stages. Sensor drift over extended deployment periods was not fully characterised. Additionally, the CNN-based plant health assessment model was trained on a limited dataset of two thousand images captured under controlled lighting conditions; its performance under variable field illumination remains unvalidated. Future work should address these gaps through longitudinal field trials and dataset expansion.

Beyond the specific contributions of this study, the findings underscore a broader principle in agricultural technology: the most impactful interventions are often those that work within existing infrastructure constraints rather than requiring wholesale replacement. Edge AI offers a viable path toward data-driven farming in precisely the contexts where it is needed most, not where connectivity is already abundant.
